rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: HSE WIS23 is practical guidance for local exhaust ventilation users in woodworking on wood-dust health risks and controls.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: The 2022 revision adds information on airflow indicators, dust lamps and improving dust control on circular saws.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: Hardwood dust can cause a rare form of nasal cancer.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: Wood dust can cause occupational asthma and may cause dermatitis.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: HSE advises dust extraction and at least dust-class M vacuum equipment for cleaning wood dust.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: For most machining and short dusty tasks, HSE identifies RPE with a minimum assigned protection factor of 20 as required.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: Cutting and sanding wood with power tools can generate significant dust levels and requires effective control.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: HSE advises effective local exhaust ventilation during MDF machining or sanding and vacuum cleaning rather than airlines or brushes.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: Wood-dust risk varies with wood type, process, dust concentration, duration, ventilation, cleaning method, RPE fit and worker susceptibility.

rows.source: HSE wood-dust exposure control
rows.verified: HSE wood-dust guidance is task-, material-, workplace-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease probability.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: Solvent-based stains, varnishes, paints, adhesives and wood-treatment chemicals can seriously affect the liver, kidneys and central nervous system.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: Dichloromethane is classed as a carcinogen and high vapour concentrations can cause unconsciousness and death.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: HSE states dichloromethane paint, varnish or lacquer stripping is restricted to industrial premises with appropriate safety measures.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: HSE recommends selecting safer materials such as waterborne products where possible.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: Extraction ventilation, suitable RPE, protective clothing and appropriate gloves may be needed for solvent work.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: Isocyanate-based products can cause asthma and dermatitis, while epoxy systems can cause dermatitis.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: Spraying reactive systems should be carried out in an enclosed spray booth or room with extraction.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: COSHH assessments should cover actual work activities, maintenance and cleaning tasks and should involve employees.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: Chemical risk varies with formulation, concentration, application method, ventilation, exposure route, duration, PPE and individual susceptibility.

rows.source: HSE woodworking solvents and reactive systems
rows.verified: HSE woodworking-chemical guidance is substance-, process-, worker-, control-, premises- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level toxicity probability.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: HSE states that wood dust can cause fire and explosion.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: The minimum explosible concentration cited for wood flour is 60 grams per cubic metre.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: Many woodworking fires start in extraction systems.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: Extraction systems should be designed so ignition, fire and explosion sources are removed or controlled.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: Frictional or attritional processing of everyday materials can create potentially combustible dust clouds.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: HSE lists sugar, coal, wood, grain, some metals and synthetic organic chemicals as examples of combustible dust materials.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: Combustible-dust control requires both prevention and mitigation of fires and explosions.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: HSG103 is directed at employers, managers, foremen and safety representatives in affected industries.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: Dust-explosion risk depends on particle size, concentration, confinement, oxygen, ignition energy, ventilation, housekeeping and equipment condition.

rows.source: HSE combustible-dust and woodworking fire control
rows.verified: HSE combustible-dust evidence is material-, process-, enclosure-, ignition-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level explosion probability.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress Management Standards
rows.verified: HSE's Management Standards use a step-by-step risk-assessment approach to work-related stress.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress Management Standards
rows.verified: The approach can use existing data, surveys and other techniques to assess the current situation.
